extracted.intended_audience: open source software project maintainers and organizational applicants seeking CZI/Wellcome/Kavli Essential Open Source Software (EOSS) grant funding for biomedical research
extracted.subtask_description: Prepare and submit a Letter of Intent (and, if invited, a Full Application) for the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative / Wellcome / Kavli 'Essential Open Source Software for Science' grant program, demonstrating the project's impact, quality, feasibility, value to biomedical users, and DEI efforts. Applications must meet scope, budget, eligibility, and reporting requirements described in the RFA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact will assess the importance of the open source software project(s) involved in the proposal to science and the open source ecosystem, in alignment with CZI’s mission to support the science and technology that will make it possible to cure, prevent, or manage all diseases by the end of the century. Reviewers will evaluate: Demonstrated scientific impact and adoption of the software project, with a particular focus on its use in biomedicine; The role of the software project in the scientific open source ecosystem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alongside qualitative materials, expert evaluation may use metrics such as: number of users and recent growth; adoption within relevant communities; number of citations or mentions of the software project in scientific literature; number of potential contributors and diversity of the organizations they represent; number of past contributions to related software projects in the relevant software stack (pushing changes upstream to dependencies, receiving changes from other nearby software projects). Include evidence of adoption/use in biomedicine and description of the project's ecosystem role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (software maturity & community)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality will assess the maturity of the software project(s), its compliance with best practices in open source development, and the existence of a healthy and diverse contributor community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will evaluate: composition and leadership of team; governance structure of the software project; software project communications and community engagement; existence, clarity, and recency of software project roadmap; clarity of process for external contributions; evidence of external contributions from outside of the core developer team (code, bug/issue reports, documentation, etc.); availability of tutorials and examples; quality and comprehensiveness of documentation. Quantitative evaluation may leverage metrics such as frequency and growth trajectory of commits over time; size and make-up of current developer team; frequency of external contributions; number of open issues and rate of issues both opened and closed; time between opening and closing of pull requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility (plan & likelihood of completion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feasibility will assess the plan of work described in the proposal and whether it can be accomplished given the requested budget and key personnel involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will evaluate: specificity and clarity of plan of work to be accomplished; proposed use of funds (relative to plan of work); likelihood of the work being accomplished; plan for tracking and validating progress against goals; degree of unmet need given existing resources; future plans for sustaining or maintaining the work funded by the grant. Provide milestones, deliverables, tracking and evaluation strategies and demonstrate appropriate alignment between budget and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value to the biomedical community
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers will evaluate the value to the biomedical community of the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: how the output of the proposal will advance project(s) adoption among biomedical researchers or produce value to their work; biomedical user needs that are unmet by the software project(s) in their current state and that will be addressed through the proposal; any improvement or integration with other tools that will improve adoption, usability, functionality, extensibility, ease of use, or performance of the project in the context of the biomedical research community. Provide concrete use-cases, user feedback, or evidence showing biomedical benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) statement
rubrics_metrics.description: All applicants invited to submit a Full Application must include in their proposal a Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DEI statement must describe (1) any efforts the software project(s) named in this proposal have undertaken to increase diversity, equity, and inclusion with respect to their contributors and audience; and (2) the results of such efforts, if applicable. This statement will be reviewed alongside other criteria. Examples of DEI statements from successful proposals are provided in prior cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope eligibility (in-scope vs out-of-scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications for two broad categories of open source software projects will be considered in scope: (1) Domain-specific software for analyzing, visualizing, and otherwise working with the specific data types that arise in biomedical science; (2) Foundational tools and infrastructure that enable a wide variety of downstream software across several domains of science and computational research (foundational tools must have demonstrated impact on some area(s) of biomedical research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software will be considered out of scope if it primarily serves domains outside biomedical science without strong evidence of adoption in biomedicine. Examples of projects less likely to be successful: a project in its earlier stages that is not used extensively or known beyond the creator(s); a project focused on improving/supporting a database or knowledge base with few community contributions or low adoption in the biomedical community; a project widely successful but with little or no applications to biomedicine; a proposal for a research project to mine, publish, or analyze research results rather than a project that will support the biomedical research process itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable Use of Funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications may request funding to support activities that maintain, grow, develop, and engage communities around essential open source software for biomedical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable uses include, but are not limited to: salary support for staff (developers, contributors, technical writers, community managers, product/project managers, UX researchers, community educators); hackathons, sprints, outreach, or other community engagement; operational needs such as cloud computing, storage, networking, continuous integration services; support for work that bridges software projects or ecosystems, including coordination across related projects. Proposals should align requested funds with the proposed activities and milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget limits & indirect costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Budget requests must fall within program-specified ranges and follow indirect cost limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications can request funding between $50,000 USD and $200,000 USD total costs per year for two years (inclusive of up to 15% for indirect/overhead costs) for an overall amount requested between $100,000 USD and $400,000 USD total costs for the two-year duration. Indirect costs cannot exceed 15% of direct costs. Budgets will be evaluated for appropriateness relative to the scope of work proposed. A detailed budget is not required at the LOI stage but will be required at the Full Application stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility & organizational requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible applicants: domestic and foreign nonprofit and for-profit organizations, public and private institutions (colleges, universities, hospitals, labs), units of state and local government, companies, and eligible agencies of the federal government. Grants are not permitted to individuals; open source projects operating independently must be affiliated with an organization (or use a fiscal sponsor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application does not come from an organization eligible to receive and distribute funds, it may designate a fiscal sponsor (e.g., NumFOCUS, Code for Science & Society). Fiscal sponsorship must be secured by the Full Application deadline. For-profit organizations may need to provide additional information and may only be eligible for funding from a subset of the funders. Non-U.S. institutions may not issue subcontracts to U.S. institutions (if funded by CZI) — be mindful when selecting applicant organization. Meta employees and Chan Zuckerberg Initiative LLC employees are not permitted to apply. The Funders reserve the right to decide applicant eligibility and request additional information at any time. Applicants must comply with OFAC, U.S. export controls, FCPA, and applicable laws; eligibility for certain funders may change if laws/regulations change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application requirements & LOI elements
rubrics_metrics.description: LOI (Letter of Intent) stage materials must be submitted through the CZI grants portal and include specified sections and details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LOI required elements: short summary of the work (max 500 words); expected value to biomedical research community (max 250 words); landscape analysis describing other tools and how this project compares (max 250 words); list of software projects to be supported and repositories/homepage URLs (up to five projects); category selection; previous funding history questions. LOIs do not need a full budget, finalized personnel list, deliverables, or institutional sign-off. Full Applications (if invited) will require description of proposed activities with milestones and deliverables; full budget; key personnel; description of recent institutional and financial support; expected outcomes plus indicators and evaluation strategies; institutional sign-off and compliance with funder grant conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process & review procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications will be evaluated by the Funders for existing impact, software quality, feasibility, expected value to the biomedical community, and the DEI statement. Evaluation uses both quantitative and qualitative factors and independent expert review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant materials will be provided by applicants and obtained by the Funders from public sources (e.g., GitHub). Independent expert review will be solicited; final decisions will be made by CZI, Wellcome and Kavli staff in consultation with expert advisors. Expert reviews will be treated confidentially and not shared with applicants. Full reviews for unsuccessful proposals may be shared with other interested funders if the applicant opts in and will be notified before sharing. Funders reserve the right to recommend no awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting & progress monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful grantees must provide annual reports and progress summaries; funders will monitor progress toward deliverables and indicators of project growth and uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual reports will include a summary of project progress that may be made publicly available. Measures of progress include indicators obtained from code repositories, issue trackers, package distribution systems, community forums, mailing lists, etc. Applicants should define indicators and evaluation strategies in the Full Application and be prepared to report them annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative selection indicators (examples of less likely successful projects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA provides specific examples of project types that are less likely to be successful in this RFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: a project in its earlier stages that is not used extensively or known beyond the creator(s); a project primarily focused on improving/supporting a database/knowledge base with few community contributions or low adoption in the biomedical community; a project widely successful but with little or no applications to biomedicine; and a proposal for a research project to mine, publish, or analyze research results rather than one that supports the biomedical research process itself. Use these as anti-patterns to assess readiness and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence sources & metrics to support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants and reviewers may use public and applicant-provided quantitative and qualitative evidence to support assessments of impact, quality, and feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested evidence includes GitHub (or other code repository) metrics, commit histories, contributor lists, issue/PR statistics, package distribution analytics, community forum activity, citations and mentions in scientific literature, user counts/growth metrics, documentation and tutorial availability, governance docs, roadmaps, and examples of external contributions. Applicants should point reviewers to these sources and provide concise summaries in the application.
